video_title: Ruchir Sharma: Why the World Is Betting on America | Podcast | In Good Company
transcript: Despite having the war in the Middle East, despite the tariffs that they have done, despite all the criticism heaped on President Trump and his policies, the anti-immigration stance, all of this has been thrown in. And yet the only country in the world where people want to put money into seems to be America. Hi everyone, I'm Nicolai Tangen, the CEO of the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund, and today I'm in really good company with Ruchir Sharma, investor, Financial Times columnist and chairman of Rockefeller International. When we spoke a year ago, Ruchir predicted that the AI bubble would end in 2026 and I promised we'd come back and check. Few people are better at challenging the crowd and I'm really looking forward to this one. So Ruchir, a warm welcome. Thanks, Nicolai. So good to be back. Absolutely, so Ruchir, has the AI bubble burst? You know, we will never really know this because there's never a point in time. If you look at all bubbles in the past, they typically tend to burst over two or three years. So now we look back at March 2000 as the turning point, we look back even at 2008, let's say March 2008 or so as the turning point where the bubble burst, but the cracks began to form in the system for many months. And my single point to you, Nicolai, when we spoke last time, exactly a year ago, was that the first signs of a bubble were forming, that if you looked at the framework that I'd outlined to you back then, the four O's that I saw, you know, like we speak about, the overvaluation, the over ownership, the over leverage, and also the fact that you're having so much over trading, which was happening in the markets. Anyway, so I'd spoken about the four O's to you back then and said that if you look at it, we are seeing that we are at a pretty advanced stage of this now being a bubble. So what are some of the more cracks you're seeing now? Yeah. But the point I'd also made back then was that bubbles don't deflate on their own. There's only one factor which deflates a bubble when the price of money goes up. That's the only factor, and we look at it… We'll come back to that. Yeah, just what are the other type of cracks you're seeing Yeah. So I think now? the big thing is rising rates, that financing is becoming much more difficult, right? Because the potential for AI to be a massive productivity boost, and, you know, the whole idea that this is going to lead to a big step up in investment, all that is playing out. But the issue is the fact that how is this going to be financed, with the question that we all, I think, seem to forget, that all these companies need external financing now to fund the AI boom. So rates have started to tick up. What is going to happen next? I think that it's, I don't see rates coming down much, right? So I think that rates have gone up. The only path which leads to a different outcome from the one that I'm predicting is the fact that we see a massive boost in productivity in the next few months, literally. And that then allows the optimism to get even higher and for rates to not go up, but for rates to come down because people sort of believe that a productivity miracle has already begun. Absent of that, I think that the path is the fact that in the next few months, the financing becomes more and more difficult and some of the big projections you have about how much CapEx is gonna be spent are gonna start coming down. I think that's the way I see it. Now, Big Tech used to pay AI out of its own pocket, and now they raise debt. Why does it worry you? As I said, now you need external financing. When you were paying it out of your own balance sheet, it was not such a big deal because you had your own cash flow, you were able to do that. Now all these companies are turning into becoming net debt. But there's one big difference in this boom, which I think is something which we have not seen in the past, which is that if you looked at the past booms, the government was not competing for capital AI today with these companies. That even if you look back at 2000 or the other instances, in fact, in 2000, the government was running a surplus. But would you say they're really competing? I mean, the tech companies are still relatively limited compared to the treasury market. Yeah, but I'm saying that's the difference, which is that you're right, that the amount of borrowing that these companies are doing now, of course, even this year, though, the amount of borrowing that the AI ecosystem has done is already 600 billion. Now you may say that's not as big as the two trillion plus deficit that the US government is running. But all these things combined together put an upward pressure on interest rates. I think that is the point that I've been making, that that's the big difference this time. And the, you know, the other point that we had spoken about with the US government's finances, which is that they really keep deteriorating, we are back to now running a budget deficit of six and a half percent of GDP, you know, so this is not something which we've seen in the past. This is an unprecedented cycle. So we can look at the past for some clues about what may happen, but the big difference this time is that the government's running a deficit of six and a half percent of GDP. That is taking away a lot of capital away from the other markets. So these deficits, it doesn't seem like the market is worrying too much about this deficit. When do you think markets will start to care? No, I think that if you look at the, and people have deconstructed this, that we have gone from interest rates of being sub 1% five years ago or so, to now interest rates of 5%, right? That's the sort of thing. A very healthy chunk of this can be explained by the persistently large deficits that the government is running. So not all of it, but at least a part of it. So it's already beginning to get priced to the stock market. The days, and for the general interest rate market, the days when you had very low interest rates which could fund everything are over. This is what I define as a regime shift, the regime of very easy money that we have is over. So financing this boom, this AI boom is going to get much more difficult. And you're right that there's no sort of alarm going on that the deficits become too large and the government still being able to finance it. But interest rates are going up at the long end as well. And a part of the reason why they're going up is because of the fact that you have much more persistent deficits that you did not have in the past. Do you read anything into the increased volatility of markets and Nasdaq? Yeah, that's usually a sign of bubbles coming to an end. That you typically, now, as I said, there are economic signs that I pointed out to you based on my four O's framework, and then you have technical signs as well, which is separate. And among the technical signs that you see is that you typically begin to see a much sharper increase in volatility towards the end of the cycle. I think that that's exactly what we're We're seeing a big step up in volatility that is happening in markets, and that usually characterizes a late stage cycle for a stock market. Now in your most recent column in the Financial Times, you talk about the world's love affair with America. Warren Buffett, he said, never bet against America, and now the mantra seems to be bet only on America. So what's going on here? Yeah, exactly. I think that this is what allows America to get away with so many other policy mistakes as well. Because I think that if you look at the last couple of years, people have been staggered that despite having the war in the Middle East, despite the tariffs that they have done, despite all the criticism heaped on President Trump and his policies, the anti-immigration stance, all of this has been thrown in. And yet the only country in the world where people want to put money into seems to be America. Why? It's because I think that never before in history have we seen that the other powers have been so weak financially. And the big sort of fault line here is China, which is that normally you would expect that China now has become the world's second largest economy. You wouldn't normally expect a fair share of global capital to be flowing into China. Yet nobody wants to invest in China, at least from a foreign investor standpoint. The amount of foreign investment in China is extremely low today. The number, and even basic stuff, the number of people today, the number of foreign people in China today is a fraction of even 1%. So this is unprecedented, which if you've never had a period of history… Do you think it will change? I see no signs of it because there's nothing that they're doing to invite more capital or to have friendlier policies. Because in fact, China, as you know, the MSCI China, which people look at, is the worst performing major stock market in the world this year. And that's because of the fact that there's so much regulatory uncertainty, there's so much overinvestment, random competition. The market structure is such where it's very hard to make money. And also because I think foreigners don't feel welcome into that country. So I think that this is a real problem that China has, but also allows America to have a longer rope. And you know, just go back to my first point that there's bubble in the American market has gotten bigger over time just because people feel there's no alternative, that they don't want to invest in. When you look at who actually owns the U .S. stock market, very high household participation, what are the reflections you have there? Well, one is the amount of retail trading going on in America today. And this is not just Americans, it's foreign as well. In fact, the big change which has happened if you look at the structure of the American market is the foreign ownership, like of the American market. That about the nearly 25% of the American market now is owned by foreigners. This number used to be sub 10% a couple of decades ago. So foreigners have really piled into the American stock market and their share has gone up significantly. And this is not just institutions, this has to do with retail investors. So I travel the world and I'm just staggered to see what the interest in the American market is in a way that it's never been. So you have cab drivers, taxi drivers in Dubai, and they're using tokens on their crypto exchanges to buy Nvidia stock. You go to Singapore and in cafes there, you have housewives opening Interactive Brokers accounts so that they can end up buying American tech stocks. So you have a retail mania around the world which is going on for American stocks. Well, our fund, 55% of the fund is invested in the US. Any reflections? No, I mean, the fact of the matter is that you are still less than the index or the average person globally, because they're, as I said, over the past year, 80% of the flows have gone into, equity flows have gone into one country, which is America. This has never happened before. You know, people come back to me and say, yeah, but because America is the world's largest economy, America's got these great tech companies, blah, blah, blah. I'm saying, yeah, but the average used to be 40%. This step up to 80% is just this decade's phenomenon. Before this decade, the average was 40%, which was America's size in the global economy is about 28% or so just now, the latest numbers. So you have this incredible disconnect that you have 28% of the global economy is America. And yet, when it comes to the equity market over the past year, 80% of flows are going into one country. And so, of course, now the comeback is that there is no other country worth investing in because China and Europe just seem so dysfunctional. And yet, I think that there's something very interesting happening here, Nicolai, which is that despite this incredible amount of flows going into America, the American stock market, interestingly, has stopped outperforming the rest of the world. Well, you said, well, last year you said that you predicted stock markets outside America to keep beating the U .S. Yeah, and I'm surprised that despite such massive flows, the American stock market, in fact, peaked in terms of its relative performance in December of 2024, and then like massively underperformed in 2025. And even in the past year, the American stock market is barely even with the international markets. So that's something interesting which is going on, which is the fact that despite the massive flows coming, the market has stopped outperforming that much. And I think that that's partly because just that because the amount of capital being guzzled here is now being used for investment, the equity issuance in this market has gone up significantly. So all these flows coming in are being guzzled by the American corporate system to fund the AI boom. Right, so buying Anthropic shares, SpaceX, that kind of thing. Exactly. Now, last year, well, we talked about the debt levels in the US, but last year we also talked about debt levels in Britain, France, and Japan. Yeah, how has this developed? Well, as you can see that, right, that everywhere interest rates have gone up at the long end. The spreads have gone up for countries running larger deficits, their spreads have gone up even more. In general, this year interest rates have gone up even more. France has been, you know, exhibit A, and I think that people forget this about this thing, France, that you can have all the ambition you want to spend, but there's a limit to it, right? right? I mean, France's government spending of the share on GDP is literally the second highest in the world after North Korea. So you just have that kind of excess going on. So I think that what we're seeing is that around the world there is greater consciousness now, at least, of the fact that these deficits are reaching unsustainable levels. The bond market isn't quite revolting, but it is at least beginning to protest. And how do you think this will pan out? I think that they just, that policymakers have zero incentive to do anything until they face a crisis. So I think that the government's spending is going to keep going up until the bond markets hit a riot point. So like even the US, we had a marginal decline in the deficit in 2025 as a share of GDP. It went back down into the fives. Now it's back into the sixes. And with the gridlock we have here now, with the Democrats controlling the Congress and you have the President Trump, the easiest compromises that they will have is allows spending to keep going up. So I see government spending the share of GDP on this upward trajectory. And sooner rather than later, the bond market will hit a riot point. But for now, it is just protesting. And so we're seeing higher and higher interest rates across the curve. What's been the biggest surprise for you this year? I think the biggest surprise for me this year has been how, you know, that as I say, that China keeps disappointing even the pessimists. I've been pessimistic about China's outlook for a while, very concerned about its debt and demographics and also its state interventionism, all those things have been concerning me and I've written extensively about it. But I would have never guessed that we have had an AI boom this year, at least for the first eight, nine months of the year. And even in that period, just how poorly China keeps doing. So the idea that China has been such a massive laggard, financially so retarded, I think has been a surprise to even a pessimist like me. And how do you tally that with a kind of the competitive strength of the Chinese corporates and technologies? It's basically technology. So I'm thinking there's a big disconnect, which is that they've obviously done very well on the technology front, but they don't know how to monetize that properly, clearly, because that's why these Chinese AI companies have not been profitable. And some of the big... I mean, you also have other technologies, right? Thinking self-driving cars, humanoids, solar, all these other things, increasing also in pharma. That's right. But everywhere it seems to be a case of over-investment, that they just throw cheap money at everything, and then you end up producing some results, but you have a massive amount of over-investment. And the other problem is the fact that China's now beginning to have a really negative effect on the rest of the world. Because in 2000s, the China was a big positive factor for the world in a couple of ways. That China then was growing very rapidly and was importing a lot of commodities and other things which ended up creating a positive spillover effect for the rest of the world. So China was doing well and pulling the rest of the world up with it. Now China's domestic economy is doing poorly and it's dragging the rest of the world down with it because what's is there's happening so much overinvestment in China and all these industries. The domestic economy cannot absorb it. So keep exporting they these surpluses, and the rest of the world faces a wave of deindustrialization. So from countries to Germany to Indonesia, their manufacturing sectors all getting hollowed out because of the incredible export surplus coming out of China. How do you read the other emerging markets? Well, I think that the, in other emerging markets, it's… Emerging markets has increasingly become a misnomer. don't know even how to classify emerging markets because if you look at the index, so to speak, half of it is Korea and Taiwan. Now, Korea and Taiwan are not emerging markets by any stretch of imagination. And they just have three to four companies which are complete lemmings of the US AI cycle. So if you're investing in emerging markets and someone has, you know, like is putting it in the index, half of it is going to Korea, Taiwan. That's not emerging market investing. That is an extension of the US AI trade. So let's get that clear. Now, the other half the of emerging markets, you really have only two large countries that make it, which is China and India. China has all these problems. India seems to be the only one, by default, which can attract large amounts of capital, has a, you know, very good corporate culture. So, but India by default is, you know, the only true emerging market in which you can put large sums of money. And it's become the opposite of AI. It's become the anti-AI trade because it doesn't have any of these AI plays. So weeks where AI is going down, India is going up. It's become negatively correlated. I mean, that's quite a bizarre situation. Why is that? Why is that? It's because I think that, you know, like India has seen to be on the other side of the AI trade for two reasons. One that at this stage of the cycle, at least in the first eight, nine months of this year, it did not have any of the AI hardware kind of stocks because India does not invest much in technology for research and development or its semiconductors, which are of a very advanced state. So that's the one reason that just from a pure listing standpoint, India did not have much of these companies or hardly any of these. Secondly, that India was seen to be a bit of a loser because of the fact that a lot of its IT services companies and others were seen to be losers in the, you know, that if the AI revolution really got going, you know, because of the fact that the services that they provide could be commoditized by AI. So when the sentiment soared for AI for at least a few weeks in the last few weeks, then you saw India bounce back very sharply because both these arguments got turned on their head. So therefore I think that that's what's happened, that India has become this anti-AI trade, both for the bad, like it was for the first eight to nine months, and for the good, like it has been for the last couple of months. So now looking into 27, what are your, how will 27 pan out? Well I'm still thinking about it, but I think that the way that I'm thinking is that the lagged effect of tighter money is going to keep showing up, which is that you're going to see I think a rise in bankruptcies, you're going to see much harder financing needs of companies to get capital, so the lagged impact of monetary policy I think is going to show up in the next 12 months or so. So that's one thing which I'm, which think I'm seeing. I the second thing, which is an extension of what I see, is that, you know, how do you prepare for this environment? I think that this is the best time, this is like, to be buying a basket of global quality stocks which have been broadly neglected in the last two, three years, but are now coming back in vogue. So I think that if you want to own any equity risk in this environment… Really? Are they really coming back in vogue? Yeah, I think that, well, they're not coming back in vogue, but they're quietly beginning to outperform. I don't know how these trends start, Nicolai. These are companies such as? These can be companies in Europe, in some emerging markets, even in beaten down markets like Brazil, Latin America, and such, across the spectrum. And very few of these are AI-facing companies. So this is the AI agnostic trade. So I think that you have India, which is the anti-AI trade, and these global quality companies, particularly there's a cohort of them. There were about 24 ,000 companies in the world which are listed, publicly listed companies. And I've come down with a list of about 250 or so of the highest quality companies trading at a relatively cheap valuation. And these, as I said, are across sectors. And less than 5% of them are in AI, are direct AI plays. I'm talking about the AI spending, AI infrastructure plays, but they are sort of across the spectrum, from financials, industrials, consumer staples. I think that having that basket for me today has become the single best investment to make for the next three to five years. Now you are both a columnist and an investor. How do you, do you split the roles, or you do both, or you're? Well, I'd say, yeah. Two hats. Yeah, well there's two hats, but I've always worn those two hats. As you know, I started writing at a young age. I mean, I started writing. Yeah, you're 17 years old, yeah? Yeah, yeah, that's right. I started writing at a very young age, and so I've done the two in parallel and my mantra has always been live life in parallel. But the two are really connected because often what I write about is my thoughts on how the world is working. What does a 17-year-old know about the world? Well, at that point in time, I started writing in India because they were just opening up to the global economy and this was 1991. And I just happened to be- And when you look at what you wrote then, what do you think? Well, I used to write about how global foreign exchange markets used to function. And I used to, when I look back at some of my writings of the early years, I'm just struck by my own courage. The ability to make bold statements and to write about stuff, which I, you know, like, today would be a bit more hesitant and I would need the crutch of a lot of data before making statements. But back then, I, you know, like you had this sort of. what's So the worst call you ever made? Well, there's a litany of those, but I'd say that I've been carried away as well. I remember in 2007, 2008, when the emerging market boom was going, all these justifications were made that emerging markets can trade at a premium to the rest of the world because of their high growth rates and stuff. And I also was swayed by that kind of logic there. So I think being carried away by these waves is what I find to be fascinating. And I do a lot of self-reflection about how to think about markets. I think there's a very important distinction that I respect markets a lot because I think that the wisdom of the crowd, there's something to it, but I think there are instances in history when the wisdom turns into a mob. And how to distinguish that crowd from a mob, I think is one of the big sort of challenges I face all the time. And that's how I face. I think that on this AI stuff, fantastic technological revolution, but you look at history, you know that this is turning into mob behavior when all the capital the world in is flowing into just one industry and sucking out money from other industries. And this also not happened before, that today what's happening is that if you're not in AI, then the other sectors, especially on the investment side, are actually seeing a flat to negative growth. It's, you know, so that, like how can the situation continue where one sector keeps sucking in all the money and the other sectors lose money, but at the end of the day, you need that sector to be buying. like all the goods that the AI ecosystem is producing. So I think this disconnect is there. But coming back to the point, the worst mistakes in investing I have made is when I've gotten sucked into the mob as well. And I think 2007, 2008, the peak of the emerging market boom has to rank as one of those instances for me. Away from business, Ruchir, what is it that you like most about New York? As I wrote a column this summer, which is that this has been a summer of the ages for New York, which is that this city has really come back in a very big way, I feel, this year. I mean, it's been a great sort of year for New York. It started with the sporting season where New York was involved in a series of victories with what's happening with the basketball front and stuff, but more than that also what happened on the World Cup fever. But, you know, it's just been a great time to be like in the city. I think it's reestablished itself as to why it's the capital of the world in a way that everyone comes here with their A game in a way. And I think that, you know, something like also interesting has happened that people in Wall Street and people other, you know, like such society tend to be caught in their own bubble of a lot of excesses, which happened in New York as well. The kind of money spent here is incredible. But the election, and I know this will sound controversial, but even someone like Mamdani getting elected, I think that ended up firing the imagination of a lot of young people in the city. As you know, a big problem in America today is the fact that a lot of the young feel disaffected by what's happening, thinking that all this wealth and all this good times are being concentrated in the hands of a few. But I think that the idea that the young felt that they had their own person now in power in a city like New York, I think also helped sentiment. So I think it's been a combination of the two coming together. So this has arguably been the best year that New York's had in a very long time and it's once again reasserted why, that people bring their A game to the city and the vibrancy and what you can do in the city is incredible. It's like a dense jungle. I mean, I walk from my home near Columbus Circle to Rockefeller Center. I don't think there's hardly a day when I don't run into someone. But you also spend time in India, right? Yes. And do you have a different personality when you're in India? I guess so, because in India I feel that it's a lot more about connecting with people, that the, it's, you know, there's a very famous anthropologist who sort of spoke about countries which are high context and low context, and I've written about this also in my first book, Breakout Nations, and I think that, I find that very fascinating, that in India it's a total high context culture. So how are you different in India compared to here? Well, I think in India, it's a much more level of informality. It's, you know, people are a lot more colorful. They speak, you know, like a lot more. Well, you're quite colorful. You're quite colorful here, too. I mean, look at your jacket. It's quite brave. I guess it's inspired by that. But I'd say that it's a much more- Like, do you walk slower and do you walk more slowly in India? No, I'd say like in India, it's just the level of informality and warmth is a lot more. And yet, there's also a downside. There've been, you know, people tell you like, when I go back to Delhi and people tell you to meet for dinner, you are meeting typically at 8 .30, 9, and eating at 10 o 'clock at night. Whereas here, 6 .30 on a working day is standard for dinner. And that's when we're having dinner tonight. Exactly, so you have to switch. You have to switch your personality virtually. But I like to do what I do in India and just do what the locals do. And when I come to New York, be a New Yorker. I think it's about adaptability. And how do you switch off here? I think that for me, my form of meditation is my running, which is that I've always been a runner. I've been a sprinter, and I've run for, I've represented India as well in the World Masters Championship for the 100 meters and 200 meters. Oh my, what's your best 100 meter? 11 .4 or so, but that was like a while ago, but I still train every evening. So even here, I think that what's non-negotiable for me is that every evening I have my coach, she herself won the bronze medal for Jamaica, you know, like a couple of decades ago in the Olympics. So she and I go back a long way and every evening I... You're in Central Park. Exactly, in Central Park we find a spot and we train for at least 60 minutes, sometimes more every evening. So for that's my me, way of, that's my form of meditation and if you can say switching off. Gee, it's pretty fast meditation if you ask me. Now, many of the young listeners want to be investors. What should they be doing? What's your advice? If I can just say, so reflecting on my own sort of career, but also key pluses and minuses, I think that the thing is the fact that, one thing which I've realized over time, that for investing, analysis is overrated, temperament is underrated. That if I look at the real successful investors over time, they have an incredibly good temperament. The ability to withstand volatility, the ability to sort of, you know, cut out noise and to have a lot of focus. Whereas on Wall Street, what seems to be in surplus is analysis. Everybody, for example, knows the valuation of a stock. It's, it's, it's like easy to do. But as I sort of say, that, borrowing from an old phrase, that a fool knows the valuation of everything but the true value of nothing. So I'd say that a lot of time is spent analyzing stuff. And a lot of people suffer from analysis paralysis. But temperament is something which I think is what very few people have. The ability, the stomach to take losses, the stomach to ride cycles, and the ability to be different and stand out from the crowd. I think- Do you think it's easier if you are on the spectrum? I think that's a very good question. I haven't thought about it that way, but possibly. Yeah, and you know some of the very famous investors, and you've interviewed them, who tend to be on the spectrum. Absolutely. Yeah. So I think that that could be a very important insight for me to think about, but yeah, this idea of temperament and how to think differently and how to stand out. Even for the last few months, the person who I sort of called my mentor was Barton Biggs. He was a very famous personality on Wall Street 20, 30 years ago. And I remember there are so many lines that he would say, and some of them would stay with me. One of them I remember he would say was, when these real booms are happening and everyone's participating in this and stuff, and he had this line that there were many sunny days when Noah was building his ark. And you think about those kind of statements, which is that, how do you sort of do something a bit different? How do you sort of not be part of the mob? So I think that that's the kind of temperament you need to have, I think, to succeed as an investor and to see through cycles. And there are many investors I know who can catch one cycle right. But very rarely are they able to catch two or three cycles correctly, or even if they get one cycle wrong, how to survive that. So temperament, I think, is the most important attribute and underestimated attribute that I know of people. But yeah, you are clearly not part of the mob. You think differently and you for sure run very fast. Thank you. Thanks, Nicolai. Great to chat with you.
